title: SLO taxonomy, capacity smoothing, and graceful degradation playbook
author: Maya Chen
content:
Summary

This playbook defines a practical SLO taxonomy, links error budgets to capacity smoothing policies, and prescribes a standardized runbook for planned and emergency graceful degradation. It is intended for service owners, SREs, and platform engineers responsible for production model-serving and user-facing features.

Why this exists

- SLOs need to map cleanly to capacity decisions and automated traffic shaping.
- Error budgets should drive predictable, transparent throttling and fallbacks—not ad-hoc firefighting.
- Teams must have a shared, low-friction procedure to degrade features while preserving critical SLAs.

Scope

- Applies to all public and internal Redwood inference endpoints and associated control planes.
- Focuses on latency and availability SLOs for tokenized inferencing, plus success-rate SLOs for control APIs (model selection, rollouts).
- Excludes long-term architectural work (e.g., major re-architectures), which should use the ADR process.

SLO taxonomy (recommended)

1) Latency SLOs (user-facing generation paths)
- p95 and p99 completion latency measured at the API gateway post-auth.
- Example: "generation.p95 < 250ms" (for interactive endpoints)

2) Availability SLOs (API success rate)
- Rolling 30d window success rate (2xx responses / total non-retryable requests).
- Example: "generation.success >= 99.9% (30d)"

3) Quality SLOs (internal, tied to evals)
- Periodic prompt set regression thresholds; tracked but not used for automated throttling.

4) Control-plane SLOs
- Model rollout operations: apply/rollback must succeed within 5 minutes 99% of the time.

Mapping SLOs to Error Budgets

- Error budget = 1 - SLO. Reserve explicit sub-budgets per consumer type (interactive vs batch) if a service handles mixed traffic.
- Example: For 99.9% availability -> monthly budget ≈ 43.8 minutes of allowable nonavailability.

Error budget consumption policy (finance-friendly)

- Normal operation: automated alerting when 25% of budget is consumed.
- Operational friction threshold: when 50% consumed, platform and product owners are notified and must schedule a remediation plan within 24 hours.
- Controlled slowdown threshold: when 75% consumed, begin gentle traffic shaping (see capacity smoothing) and enable degraded-mode flags.
- Emergency threshold: when 90% consumed, activate emergency degradation playbook (Section: Degradation runbook).

Capacity smoothing policy

Purpose: Avoid large-scale autoscale events and noisy neighbor spikes by smoothing demand and preemptively shifting traffic to cheaper/less-loaded variants.

Policy primitives:
- Token leaky-bucket queueing at the edge with per-route burst window (default 2s)
- Adaptive per-route concurrency caps; target headroom = 20% of reserved capacity for Dedicated pools
- Soft-steering rules: route < X% traffic to lower-capacity region/model variant when 75% of capacity reached

Decision matrix (summary):
- Utilization < 60%: normal routing, encourage consolidation for cost efficiency.
- Utilization 60–80%: enable predictive pre-warm and lower-cost model recommendations via Redwood Optimize suggestions.
- Utilization 80–92%: begin soft-steering and enable prefix caching aggressively.
- Utilization > 92%: trigger emergency throttles and graceful degradation.

Degradation runbook (step-by-step)

Preconditions: Triggered if error budget > 90% consumed or utilization > 92% sustained for 5 minutes.

1) Triage and declare impact level (S, M, L)
   - S: single-region, single-customer impact.
   - M: multi-region or multi-customer partial degradation.
   - L: global outage or severe performance across many customers.

2) Notify stakeholders (automated paging + Slack channel)
   - Use paging channel: #pager-service-<service-name> and tag oncall.

3) Immediate mitigations (first 10 minutes)
   - Reduce per-request token limits by 25% (if supported) via API gateway header injection.
   - Switch non-critical routes to cached-responses mode.
   - Apply client-side 429 backpressure with Retry-After guidance for best-effort clients.

4) Capacity actions (10–30 minutes)
   - Increase Dedicated pool burst capacity (pre-configured reserve) by 1 notch.
   - Hot-add N instances to autoscaling group if possible (documented per-region).
   - If hardware-unavailable, enable lower-precision quantized model variant for non-critical tenants.

5) Controlled degrade (30+ minutes)
   - Enable feature-flagged degraded experience: e.g., disable streaming and fall back to final-response only; reduce max tokens; disable non-essential model tools.
   - Update status page and customer comms templates (see Appendix).

6) Monitor and declare recovery window
   - When both utilization < 70% and error budget drift reverses for two consecutive 15-minute buckets, begin staged rollback of degradations.

Observability and thresholds (signals to monitor)

- Primary metrics:
  - request_latency_p95_ms, request_latency_p99_ms
  - request_success_rate_30d
  - token_throughput_per_gpu, kv_cache_hit_ratio
  - request_queue_length_edge, per-route_concurrency

- Key alert thresholds (examples):
  - p95 > SLO * 1.3 for 3m -> SEV2
  - p99 > SLO * 2 for 3m -> SEV1
  - sustained queue length > 50 for 5m -> SEV2
  - capacity_utilization > 92% for 5m -> SEV1

Operational tooling patterns and recipes

1) Emergency throttle via API gateway (CLI example)
```
# throttle route to 60 rps
redwoodctl gateway throttle set --route /v1/generation --rate 60
```

2) Short-lived feature flag for degraded mode (YAML config snippet)
```
feature_flag:
  name: generation-degraded-mode
  scope: service:generation
  enabled: true
  reason: "Emergency degradation: high utilization"
  controls:
    - reduce_streaming: true
    - max_tokens: 512
```

3) Autoscale dry-run command (idempotent)
```
redwoodctl capacity dry-run --pool dedicated-west-1 --instances +4 --reason "preemptive smooth"
```

Incident review and evidence checklist

Required artifacts for every degradation incident:
- Alert timeline (from pager and alerting system)
- Graphs (p95/p99, utilization, queue length, token throughput) clipped to ±3 hours of incident start
- Deployment and rollout history for 24 hours prior
- Error budget burn rate calculation and per-tenant impact table
- Runbook actions executed (who, when, commands run)

Retention policy table

| Artifact | Retention | Owner | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Raw telemetry (high-res) | 30 days | eng-sre | High fidelity for investigations |
| Aggregated metrics | 365 days | eng-sre | For trend analysis |
| Incident timeline | 3 years | eng-sre | Required for post-incident audits |
| Runbook execution logs | 2 years | service-owner | Includes redwoodctl command history |

Post-incident review (90-minute template)

- Opening (5m): incident impact summary and owner
- Timeline walk (20m): factual sequence of detection, mitigation, recovery
- Root cause hypothesis (20m): technical and organizational contributors
- Action items (20m): clearly assigned, with due dates and verification criteria
- Readout and comms (10m): internal + customer messaging decisions
- Review close (15m): sign-off from SRE lead and product owner

Runbook ownership and lifecycle

- Every runbook must have a named owner (documented in the space). Owner responsibilities:
  - Keep SLO definitions and thresholds current each quarter.
  - Run a tabletop quarterly with production traffic replay.
  - Maintain playbook commands and dry-run scripts.

Templates and appendices

- Sample JSON SLO definition (compatible with SLO service):
```
{
  "service": "generation",
  "slo": {
    "name": "generation.p95",
    "target": 0.95,
    "window_days": 30
  }
}
```

- Prometheus-style alert example:
```
alert: GenerationP95High
expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(api_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, route)) > 0.25
for: 3m
labels:
  severity: page
annotations:
  summary: "generation p95 latency exceeded threshold"
```

- Customer comms template (status page summary):
"We are experiencing elevated latency for the Generation API affecting a subset of customers. Engineering is actively mitigating and we will provide updates every 30 minutes. Expected impact: reduced throughput for non-critical requests."
